An autonomous car that drives a square and steers itself straight

A scale vehicle built around an STM32 microcontroller, with PID heading control, obstacle stopping and live telemetry, for a challenge with John Deere.

Team project, built with three classmates
Author
Diego Becerra Fuentes
Course
Industrial Automation, Tec de Monterrey
Delivered
December 2025

The route in one loop: four corners, a pause at each, and a stop if something gets in the way.

The challenge

The brief came from an educational collaboration with John Deere: build a scale vehicle that drives a square by itself and sends data back as it goes. The project also supports UN Sustainable Development Goal 9, industry, innovation and infrastructure, since it pushed us to learn an unfamiliar microcontroller and combine what we had studied.

Navigate

Visit four corners of a square, 1 to 10 m per side, in order, pausing 10 seconds at each.

Stop for obstacles

Brake when something blocks the way and continue once the path is clear.

Close the loop

Regulate speed and steering with feedback so the motion stays smooth.

Report back

Stream speed, direction, position and status to a computer in real time.

The vehicle

We first chose the motors, 12 V DC units with encoders, then modeled the chassis in SolidWorks. The base plates are cut from MDF and the supports are 3D-printed in PLA. A differential drive lets each side turn at its own speed, so the outer wheel can travel farther in a curve without slipping.

Microcontroller setup and pin map

Timer 1 generates the motor PWM, I2C reads the MPU6050, and USART1 carries Bluetooth telemetry and commands. Encoder edges are caught with external interrupts.

Encoder 2 A, BPA4, PB3Wheel 2 pulses

How it steers

A single closed loop does the hard work: heading. The MPU6050 reports yaw, a PID controller compares it with the target angle, and its output is added to one wheel’s speed and subtracted from the other’s. With a base speed of 50% and a correction of 10%, the wheels run at 60% and 40%, so the car turns back on course without losing much forward speed.

left  = base_pct + pid_out
right = base_pct - pid_out      // both clamped to 0..100%

Kp = 3.0

The immediate push against large errors.

Ki = 0.10

Removes leftover error from motor asymmetry or sensor bias.

Kd = 0.80

Damps the response to avoid oscillation.

3° dead zone

Ignores tiny errors, saving motor wear and noise.

Yaw wraps around at 360°, so the error is always taken the short way: going from 10° to 350° becomes a 20° left turn, not a 340° right one.

Distance is simpler. Each wheel gives 452 pulses per turn, so a 6.5 cm wheel resolves about 0.45 mm per pulse. When the pulse count reaches the target for the chosen side, the car stops and moves to the next state. Speed is set with a fixed PWM duty, with no feedback loop.

Process variable, setpoint and output for each loop
LoopProcess variableSetpointOutput
Heading (closed loop)Filtered yaw angleTarget yaw, 0 to 360°Differential speed correction, ±100%
Distance (threshold)Encoder pulses since the side beganPulses for the chosen side lengthSwitch to the pause state
Base speed (open loop)Measured speed, for telemetry onlySpeed percentage, 0 to 100%Fixed PWM duty cycle

The software

The firmware is a state machine, which kept it clear and easy to change. Each side of the square repeats the same cycle, and after the fourth side the car stops.

MovethenStopthenPause 10 sthenTurn 90°repeat 4 times

The ultrasonic sensor is checked in both the automatic and manual modes. An obstacle closer than 15 cm puts the car in an obstacle state and sends a message to the interface. At each corner the car resets its yaw to zero and turns 90° from there.

Manual commands over Bluetooth
  • A, B, C, D, E: forward, back, stop, right, left.
  • F, G, S: set side length (10 to 1000 cm), turn angle and speed percentage.
  • R, U, V, T: reset encoder pulses, read distance, show speed, show angle.
  • Z: reset the yaw reference to zero.

Telemetry interface

We built a control panel in MATLAB App Designer. It connects over the Bluetooth serial port, shows speed, yaw, error, route progress and obstacle distance in real time, and lets you tune the PID gains and start a square from the same screen.

Interface panels
PanelWhat it does
ConnectionPick the port and see connected or disconnected
Progress lightsShow which side of the square the car is on
Yaw monitorRadial gauge with current yaw, target, error and a reset
PID gainsSet and apply Kp, Ki and Kd live
SpeedSet PWM percent (the motors only start above 50%) and read speed in cm/s
Square routeSet the side length in meters and start
SensorsShow ultrasonic distance and reset the encoder
StopBrake the car manually

Test run

Testing focused on three things: the PID heading, the accuracy of the closed square, and the telemetry.

  • Tuning Kp, Ki and Kd took many iterations, because the car reacted strongly to small disturbances. Once tuned, it held a straight line before each programmed turn.
  • With heading correction active, the car followed the route geometry and ended where it started.
  • The ultrasonic sensor reliably stopped the car for obstacles closer than 15 cm.
  • Interface readings matched the car’s real behavior.

An outdoor test run of the car.

What I took away

Mechanical precision alone does not give a straight line. Motors are never identical and floors are never perfect, so without correcting heading in real time the error piles up until the car is well off its route. A tuned PID turned a mechanically imperfect car into one that follows angle references reliably.

Each sensor played its own part: encoders for distance, the MPU6050 for orientation, and the ultrasonic sensor for safety, without slowing the main control loop. Telemetry let us check hypotheses with data instead of by eye.

Personally, the state machine was the most useful lesson. Splitting the logic into states such as moving, turning and stopping for an obstacle made the code simpler and much easier to extend. Building the whole system, mechanics, electronics, logic and control, made me feel stronger as a mechatronics engineer.

As a team we also learned a new microcontroller and its configuration, PWM, UART, I2C, timers, Bluetooth and PID control.
